passage: The plan on Aadhya's wall had four lines: build the software, sign the hospital chain, hire staff, grow. Irawati, the co-founder, kept asking how they would get the chain to sign. "They will," said Aadhya. "Their head of IT loved the demo." Nothing else was written down, no second customer, no smaller clinics. Months went by. The chain's pilot began, and then stalled: procurement wanted new forms, then a security review, then a budget approval next quarter. In the last six weeks of cash, Aadhya and Irawati rang clinics they had never called, and stayed at the office until midnight. Nobody picked up quickly. On the last Friday Irawati said quietly, "We should have had a plan B in March."

qa.q: What held up the hospital chain's pilot?
qa.a: Procurement wanted new forms, then a security review, then a budget approval next quarter.

qa.q: What does Aadhya's "They will" suggest about how Aadhya feels?
qa.a: It suggests Aadhya feels confident and hopeful, placing trust in the head of IT's reaction to the demo.

qa.q: What could the founders have done differently?
qa.a: They could have lined up several smaller customers, such as clinics, alongside the hospital chain so one delay would not sink them.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel on the last Friday?
qa.a: Irawati probably feels anxious and regretful, wishing a plan B had existed earlier.

grounding: Aadhya keeps the plan vague and assumes a hospital chain will sign, and the team scrambles with no plan B when the pilot stalls.

"Any news from the hospital chain?" Nazia asked, not looking up from her laptop.
"Their purchase team wants another round of paperwork," Tenzin said. "They said 'end of quarter' again."
"Tenzin, that's what they said in March. It's August. We have six weeks of money left."
"The pilot doctors love it. They'll sign."
"The doctors don't sign. Purchase signs. What's our plan if they don't?"
Silence.
"We don't have one, do we?"
"I thought we wouldn't need one. One contract with them and we'd be set for two years."
"So for five months we talked to nobody else." Nazia shut her laptop. "Okay. Tonight we list every small clinic in the city. Tomorrow we start calling. Six weeks."
Tenzin rubbed his face. "I really believed it."
"I know. So did I, a bit."

qa.q: How much money did they have left?
What was Tenzin feeling when he said "I really believed it"?
qa.a: He felt deflated and a little ashamed, realising hope had taken the place of a plan.

qa.q: What could they have done back in March?
qa.a: Kept talking to small clinics as a plan B while the hospital pilot worked its way through purchasing.

qa.q: How does Nazia experience the situation?
qa.a: Nazia is frustrated and alarmed, but moves straight into action and admits she half-believed it too.

grounding: It shows a founder assuming one hospital chain would sign, so when the pilot stalls in purchasing there is no plan B and the team scrambles in the last weeks.

subtype: Approach: hoping a big customer will appear [Pitfall]
passage:
For most of last year our whole plan fit in one sentence: "When the hospital chain signs, we're fine." Yusuf and I had built a tool for tracking surgical supplies, and the chain's head nurse loved the pilot. Every call ended with "We'll move to purchase soon."
So I never wrote a proper plan. Why would I? One contract would cover us for years.
In October the chain's purchase department asked for a security audit we had never heard of, then went quiet. We had seven weeks of money. Yusuf and I spent those weeks cold-calling every small nursing home in Jaipur, begging for trials, sleeping four hours a night. We signed two, just barely enough.
What I'd do differently: from the first month, a plan B with real names on it. Hoping is what I did instead of planning.
— Hansa

qa.q: What did the chain's purchase department ask for?
qa.a: A security audit they had never heard of.

qa.q: How did Hansa feel during the seven weeks of cold-calling?
qa.a: Hansa felt desperate and exhausted, begging for trials on four hours' sleep.

qa.q: What would Hansa do differently now?
qa.a: Keep a plan B from the first month, with the real names of smaller customers to approach.

qa.q: How might Yusuf have experienced relying on the one contract?
qa.a: Yusuf was dragged into the last-minute scramble too, cold-calling and losing sleep because there was no backup.

grounding: It shows a founder keeping the plan vague while waiting on one hospital chain, so when the deal stalls in purchasing the team scrambles with no plan B.
